title: Εἴδωλον καὶ Λόχος
titleEn: The Vigil and the Ambush — Odyssey 4.742–847
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Eurycleia, the old nurse, calms Penelope's grief and confesses that she alone has known of Telemachus's voyage, urging Penelope to wash, pray to Athena, and trust that the gods will not let the line of Odysseus die out entirely. Penelope prays for her son's safety, and Athena hears her. In the hall the suitors, overhearing one of their own boast carelessly of the plot against Telemachus, are sharply hushed by Antinous, and twenty of them arm a swift ship and put out to lie in wait near the island of Asteris. Penelope, fasting and torn between hope and fear for her son, falls asleep, and Athena sends a phantom in the likeness of her sister Iphthime to comfort her in a dream. The phantom promises that Telemachus, under Athena's own protection, will come to no harm, but slips away through the door-bolt without saying plainly whether Odysseus himself still lives. Penelope wakes warmed by the vivid dream, while offshore the suitors take up their ambush in the strait by rocky Asteris.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε φίλη τροφὸς Εὐρύκλεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe philē trophos Eurykleia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed the dear nurse Eurycleia:
sentences.i: Then her dear nurse Eurycleia spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: προσέειπε is the aorist of προσαυδάω, 'addressed'; τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is the same reply-formula already fixed for the masculine τόν ('Him then in turn addressed'), here adapted to the feminine τήν since Penelope was the one just addressed. φίλη τροφός, 'dear nurse', is Eurycleia's standing periphrasis: she is the old slave-woman who nursed both Odysseus and Telemachus, and now comforts the weeping Penelope. Her name, new to this part, takes the familiar English form Eurycleia throughout.

sentences.t:
νύμφα φίλη, σὺ μὲν ἄρ με κατάκτανε νηλέι χαλκῷ
ἢ ἔα ἐν μεγάρῳ·
sentences.tr:
nympha philē, sy men ar me kataktane nēlei chalkōi
ē ea en megarōi·
sentences.l:
“Dear bride, you then indeed kill me with pitiless bronze,
or leave me in the hall;
sentences.i: “Dear lady, kill me yourself outright with pitiless bronze, or leave me here in the hall;
sentences.n: νύμφα, literally 'young wife, bride', is here an affectionate title an old family retainer uses for her mistress; Eurycleia nursed Penelope's husband and speaks to her almost as a daughter. κατάκτανε is the aorist imperative of κατακτείνω 'kill outright'; νηλέι χαλκῷ, 'with pitiless bronze', is a stock phrase for a death-blow, χαλκός standing for the weapon itself. ἔα is the imperative of ἐάω 'let be, allow'. Eurycleia dramatically stakes her own life on what she is about to confess, since she broke faith with her oath to serve Penelope.

sentences.t: μῦθον δέ τοι οὐκ ἐπικεύσω.
sentences.tr: mython de toi ouk epikeusō.
sentences.l: but the matter to you I will not hide.
sentences.i: for I will not hide the matter from you.
sentences.n: ἐπικεύσω is the future of ἐπικεύθω, 'hide, conceal further', built on κεύθω with the intensive prefix ἐπι-. τοι is the enclitic dative of σύ, 'to you', extremely common in direct address. μῦθος here means simply 'the story, the matter', not yet the later sense 'myth'. Eurycleia moves at once from her dramatic offer of death to her real purpose: confessing what she has concealed until now.

sentences.t:
ᾔδε’ ἐγὼ τάδε πάντα, πόρον δέ οἱ ὅσσ’ ἐκέλευε,
σῖτον καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.tr:
ēide’ egō tade panta, poron de hoi hoss’ ekeleue,
siton kai methy hēdy·
sentences.l:
I knew all these things, and I gave him whatever he bade,
food and sweet wine;
sentences.i: I knew all this, and I gave him whatever he asked for, food and sweet wine;
sentences.n: ᾔδε’ is ᾔδεα, a pluperfect of οἶδα used with past sense (just as the perfect οἶδα itself has present sense, 'I know', its pluperfect regularly has past sense), 'I knew'. πόρον is the unaugmented aorist of a defective verb (no present in use), 'gave, provided'; οἱ is 'to him', Telemachus; ἐκέλευε is an imperfect, 'kept bidding'. This is the reader's first confirmation that Eurycleia alone helped provision Telemachus's secret voyage to Pylos and Sparta.

sentences.t:
ἐμεῦ δ’ ἕλετο μέγαν ὅρκον
μὴ πρὶν σοὶ ἐρέειν, πρὶν δωδεκάτην γε γενέσθαι
ἢ σ’ αὐτὴν ποθέσαι καὶ ἀφορμηθέντος ἀκοῦσαι,
ὡς ἂν μὴ κλαίουσα κατὰ χρόα καλὸν ἰάπτῃς.
sentences.tr:
emeu d’ heleto megan horkon
mē prin soi ereein, prin dōdekatēn ge genesthai
ē s’ autēn pothesai kai aphormēthentos akousai,
hōs an mē klaiousa kata chroa kalon iaptēis.
sentences.l:
and from me he took a great oath
not to tell you before, before the twelfth day should come,
or you yourself should miss him and hear of his setting-out,
so that not weeping you might mar your fair skin.
sentences.i: and he made me swear a great oath not to tell you before the twelfth day came, or before you missed him yourself and heard he had gone, so that you would not mar your fair skin with weeping.
sentences.n: ἕλετο is the unaugmented aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'took (an oath from me)'. ἐρέειν is an uncontracted future infinitive, 'to tell' (Attic ἐρεῖν); ἀφορμηθέντος is an aorist passive participle of ἀφορμάω, 'having set out'. ἰάπτῃς is a subjunctive of ἰάπτω 'harm, mar'; κατὰ χρόα καλόν, 'over your fair skin', is a stock phrase for the damage tears and grief were thought to do to a mourner's looks.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὑδρηναμένη, καθαρὰ χροῒ εἵμαθ’ ἑλοῦσα,
εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀναβᾶσα σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξὶν
εὔχε’ Ἀθηναίῃ κούρῃ Διὸς αἰγιόχοιο·
sentences.tr:
all’ hydrēnamenē, kathara chroï heimath’ helousa,
eis hyperōi’ anabasa syn amphipoloisi gynaixin
euche’ Athēnaiēi kourēi Dios aigiochoio·
sentences.i: But wash yourself, put on clean clothing, go up to your upper room with your attendant women, and pray to Athena, the daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus;
sentences.n: ὑδρηναμένη is an aorist middle participle, 'having washed oneself, bathed'; here, as often, aorist participles carry imperative force alongside the true imperative εὔχεο, 'pray!' ὑπερῶιον is the women's upper chamber. αἰγιόχοιο Zeus, 'aegis-bearing Zeus', is the standing genitive epithet. This same line, all but identical, will describe Penelope actually doing as Eurycleia says at 759–760.

sentences.t: ἡ γάρ κέν μιν ἔπειτα καὶ ἐκ θανάτοιο σαώσαι.
sentences.tr: hē gar ken min epeita kai ek thanatoio saōsai.
sentences.l: for she then might save him even out of death.
sentences.i: for she may yet save him, even from death.
sentences.n: κέν is ἄν, marking the potential optative σαώσαι (aorist optative of σῴζω/σαόω); μιν is 'him', Telemachus. The line states plainly why Eurycleia urges the prayer: even death itself is not beyond a goddess's power to avert.

sentences.t: μηδὲ γέροντα κάκου κεκακωμένον·
sentences.tr: mēde geronta kakou kekakōmenon·
sentences.l: nor the old man, with misery already worn down;
sentences.i: and do not trouble the old man either, worn down with grief as he already is;
sentences.n: The clause is compressed, with no verb expressed: γέροντα is Laertes, Odysseus's father, called simply 'the old man'; κάκου, a genitive of κακόν 'ill, trouble', goes with the perfect passive participle κεκακωμένον, 'worn down, afflicted' (from κακόω). Continuing the negative force of the clauses above, the sense is that Penelope should not go and burden the old man, already broken by grief, with the news either. Such ellipsis of a governing verb is common in urgent, compressed Homeric speech.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὀίω
πάγχυ θεοῖς μακάρεσσι γονὴν Ἀρκεισιάδαο
ἔχθεσθ’, ἀλλ’ ἔτι πού τις ἐπέσσεται ὅς κεν ἔχῃσι
δώματά θ’ ὑψερεφέα καὶ ἀπόπροθι πίονας ἀγρούς.
sentences.tr:
ou gar oiō
panchy theois makaressi gonēn Arkeisiadao
echthesth’, all’ eti pou tis epessetai hos ken echēisi
dōmata th’ hypserephea kai apoprothi pionas agrous.
sentences.l:
for I do not think
that altogether to the blessed gods the offspring of Arceisius' son
is hateful, but still somewhere there will be one who shall hold
the high-roofed halls and the rich fields far off.”
sentences.i: for I do not think that the blessed gods utterly hate the line of Arceisius' son, but that there will still be someone left to hold the high-roofed house and the rich fields far away.”
sentences.n: ὀίω is 'I think' (Attic οἴομαι), an epic uncontracted present form of the ordinary thematic verb οἴομαι, not itself athematic; ἔχθεσθ’ governs the dative θεοῖς μακάρεσσι, 'be hateful to'. Γονὴν Ἀρκεισιάδαο, 'the offspring of the son of Arceisius', names Laertes by his patronymic and so designates the whole family line of Odysseus, of which Telemachus is the one living hope. ἐπέσσεται is future of ἔπειμι, 'will exist hereafter'; ὑψερεφής 'high-roofed' is a formulaic epithet of a great house.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῆς δ’ εὔνησε γόον, σχέθε δ’ ὄσσε γόοιο.
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tēs d’ eunēse goon, schethe d’ osse gooio.
sentences.l: So she spoke, and lulled her lament, and checked her eyes from weeping.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and calmed Penelope's grief, and stopped the tears in her eyes.
sentences.n: φάτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of φημί, the regular epic speech-closing verb, elsewhere fixed as 'So he spoke'; since the speaker here is a woman, 'she' takes the place of 'he' in the same construction. εὔνησε is aorist of εὐνάω 'put to sleep, lull', a vivid metaphor for calming grief; σχέθε is an unaugmented aorist of ἔχω, 'held, checked'; ὄσσε is the old dual 'the two eyes', with γόοιο as a genitive of separation, 'from weeping'.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὑδρηναμένη, καθαρὰ χροῒ εἵμαθ’ ἑλοῦσα
εἰς ὑπερῷ’ ἀνέβαινε σὺν ἀμφιπόλοισι γυναιξίν,
ἐν δ’ ἔθετ’ οὐλοχύτας κανέῳ, ἠρᾶτο δ’ Ἀθήνῃ·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ hydrēnamenē, kathara chroï heimath’ helousa
eis hyperōi’ anebaine syn amphipoloisi gynaixin,
en d’ ethet’ oulochytas kaneōi, ērato d’ Athēnēi·
sentences.i: She washed, put on clean clothing, went up to her upper room with her attendant women, put barley-grains in a basket, and prayed to Athena;
sentences.n: This narrates Penelope carrying out Eurycleia's instructions almost word for word: ὑδρηναμένη, καθαρὰ χροῒ εἵμαθ’ ἑλοῦσα repeats 750 verbatim, a small formal proof of obedience typical of Homeric command-and-execution scenes. οὐλοχύται are the barley-grains regularly scattered at the start of a sacrifice or formal prayer, used here even though no animal is killed. ἠρᾶτο is imperfect middle of ἀράομαι, 'pray, vow'.

sentences.t:
κλῦθί μευ, αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος, Ἀτρυτώνη,
εἴ ποτέ τοι πολύμητις ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἢ βοὸς ἢ ὄϊος κατὰ πίονα μηρί’ ἔκηε,
sentences.tr:
klythi meu, aigiochoio Dios tekos, Atrytōnē,
ei pote toi polymētis eni megaroisin Odysseus
ē boos ē oïos kata piona mēri’ ekēe,
sentences.l:
“Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone,
if ever to you, in his halls, many-wiled Odysseus
of an ox or of a sheep burned fat thigh-pieces,
sentences.i: “Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, Atrytone: if ever Odysseus, the man of many wiles, burned for you the fat thigh-pieces of an ox or a sheep in his halls,
sentences.n: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear'. Ἀτρυτώνη, 'Atrytone', is a cult-title of Athena, traditionally derived as 'the Unwearied' (ἀ- privative and τρύω 'wear out'), though the formation is irregular and the sense is not certain; it is kept here as a transliterated name. πολύμητις 'many-wiled' is Odysseus's fixed epithet. The conditional recalls a standard Homeric prayer-form, reminding a god of past sacrifices as grounds for a favor now; μηρία are the fat-wrapped thigh-bones burned as the god's portion.

sentences.t:
τῶν νῦν μοι μνῆσαι, καί μοι φίλον υἷα σάωσον,
μνηστῆρας δ’ ἀπάλαλκε κακῶς ὑπερηνορέοντας.
sentences.tr:
tōn nyn moi mnēsai, kai moi philon huia saōson,
mnēstēras d’ apalalke kakōs hyperēnoreontas.
sentences.l:
of these things now for me be mindful, and save for me my dear son,
and ward off the suitors, evilly overweening.”
sentences.i: remember these things now for my sake, and save my dear son, and ward off the suitors in their evil arrogance.”
sentences.n: μνῆσαι is an aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκομαι, 'be mindful of', governing the genitive τῶν. σάωσον is an aorist imperative of σαόω/σῴζω, 'save'; ἀπάλαλκε is an old reduplicated aorist imperative, 'ward off, defend against'. ὑπερηνορέοντας, 'being overweening', describes the suitors' presumption, and the same root recurs of them at 769; a related but distinct adjective, ὑπερφίαλος, is used of them at 774 and 790.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ὀλόλυξε, θεὰ δέ οἱ ἔκλυεν ἀρῆς.
sentences.tr: hōs eipous’ ololyxe, thea de hoi eklyen arēs.
sentences.l: So having spoken she cried aloud, and the goddess heard her prayer.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and raised the ritual cry, and the goddess heard her prayer.
sentences.n: εἰποῦσα is the feminine aorist participle 'having said', the regular counterpart of the masculine ὡς εἰπών. ὀλολύζω is properly the ritual cry raised by women at prayer or sacrifice, not simple weeping; κλύω governs the genitive ἀρῆς, 'heard her prayer'. The line closes the prayer scene and signals, within the narrative itself, that Athena will act for Penelope.

sentences.t: μνηστῆρες δ’ ὁμάδησαν ἀνὰ μέγαρα σκιόεντα·
sentences.tr: mnēstēres d’ homadēsan ana megara skioenta·
sentences.l: And the suitors made an uproar throughout the shadowy hall;
sentences.i: The suitors broke into uproar throughout the shadowy hall.
sentences.n: This half-line already stood whole, with a different second line, in an earlier part; the shared wording is kept unchanged here. ὁμαδέω 'make a din, uproar' describes the suitors reacting to the cry they have just heard from within; σκιόεις 'shadowy' is a standing epithet of the great hall, lit by fire but still dim in its recesses.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.tr: hōde de tis eipeske neōn hyperēnoreontōn·
sentences.l: Thus would someone say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: and one of the overbearing young men would say something like this:
sentences.n: εἴπεσκε is an iterative imperfect in -σκε, 'would keep saying', marking a repeated, typical reaction rather than one moment; ὑπερηνορεόντων echoes the very word Penelope has just used of these same young men in her prayer (766). This whole line already stood, unchanged, in an earlier part, describing the suitors gossiping about Telemachus's departure, and the wording is repeated verbatim.

sentences.t:
ἦ μάλα δὴ γάμον ἄμμι πολυμνήστη βασίλεια
ἀρτύει, οὐδέ τι οἶδεν ὅ οἱ φόνος υἷι τέτυκται.
sentences.tr:
ē mala dē gamon ammi polymnēstē basileia
artyei, oude ti oiden ho hoi phonos huii tetyktai.
sentences.l:
“Surely now indeed a marriage for us the much-wooed queen
is preparing, nor at all does she know that for her son death has been contrived.”
sentences.i: “Surely the much-wooed queen is now preparing a marriage for one of us, and she has no idea that death has been arranged for her son.”
sentences.n: ἦ μάλα δή is an emphatic, often ironic opening, 'surely now indeed'. πολυμνήστη, 'much-wooed', puns on μνηστῆρες 'suitors' and μνάομαι 'woo'; ἀρτύει 'is preparing, arranging'. τέτυκται is a perfect passive of τεύχω, 'has been wrought, contrived', with φόνος 'murder' as subject: an unnamed suitor's careless boast lets slip, mid-sentence, the very plot the group has been at pains to keep secret.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα τις εἴπεσκε, τὰ δ’ οὐκ ἴσαν ὡς ἐτέτυκτο.
sentences.tr: hōs ara tis eipeske, ta d’ ouk isan hōs etetykto.
sentences.l: So then someone would say, but they did not know how it had been contrived.
sentences.i: So one of them would say, not knowing how matters really stood.
sentences.n: ἴσαν is an unaugmented pluperfect-with-imperfect-sense of οἶδα, 'they knew' (Attic ἤδεσαν); ἐτέτυκτο, pluperfect passive of τεύχω, echoes τέτυκται in the line just spoken — the suitors do not realize their own idle remark has stumbled onto the truth of the very plot some of them are hatching. τά is a neuter plural pronoun, 'these things, the facts'.

sentences.t: τοῖσιν δ’ Ἀντίνοος ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.tr: toisin d’ Antinoos agorēsato kai meteeipe·
sentences.l: And Antinous addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: And Antinous addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπε is the house-fixed formula already used elsewhere of Antinous taking the floor. ἀγοράομαι is a denominative verb from ἀγορή 'assembly, gathering', 'make a speech to it'; μετέειπε, from μετεῖπον, is 'spoke among (them)', with τοῖσιν as its dative. Antinous moves at once to silence the man whose remark has just given away too much.

sentences.t:
δαιμόνιοι, μύθους μὲν ὑπερφιάλους ἀλέασθε
πάντας ὁμῶς, μή πού τις ἀπαγγείλῃσι καὶ εἴσω.
sentences.tr:
daimonioi, mythous men hyperphialous aleasthe
pantas homōs, mē pou tis apangeilēisi kai eisō.
sentences.l:
“Madmen, from overweening words refrain,
all of you alike, lest someone report it even within.
sentences.i: “You fools, keep away from such reckless talk, all of you alike, in case someone carries word of it inside.
sentences.n: δαιμόνιοι is a vocative of rebuke, 'you strange, mad creatures', not a compliment; ἀλέασθε is an aorist imperative middle of ἀλέομαι 'avoid, shun'. ὑπερφίαλος 'overweening, presumptuous' describes the suitors' own careless talk, and the same root recurs of them at 790; a related but distinct adjective, ὑπερηνορέων, was applied to them at 766 and 769. ἀπαγγείλῃσι is a subjunctive in -ησι after μή ... τις in a fear-clause; εἴσω, 'within, indoors', means specifically inside the house, to Penelope.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε σιγῇ τοῖον ἀναστάντες τελέωμεν
μῦθον, ὃ δὴ καὶ πᾶσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ἤραρεν ἡμῖν.
sentences.tr:
all’ age sigēi toion anastantes teleōmen
mython, ho dē kai pasin eni phresin ēraren hēmin.
sentences.l:
But come, in silence, having risen, let us accomplish
this plan, which indeed has fitted in the minds of us all.”
sentences.i: let us rise up and carry it out in silence, this plan that has found favor with the minds of all of us.”
sentences.n: σιγῇ, 'in silence', is a dative of manner; τελέωμεν is a hortatory subjunctive of τελέω, 'accomplish, bring to completion'. ἤραρεν is the reduplicated second aorist of ἀραρίσκω, 'fit, join together' (the augment fuses into the reduplication, ἀρ-αρ- → ἤραρ-), used figuratively of a plan that 'fits' every mind alike — the same verb underlying the noun ἁρμονία. μῦθον again means 'the plan agreed on' rather than 'speech'.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐκρίνατ’ ἐείκοσι φῶτας ἀρίστους,
βὰν δ’ ἰέναι ἐπὶ νῆα θοὴν καὶ θῖνα θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn ekrinat’ eeikosi phōtas aristous,
ban d’ ienai epi nēa thoēn kai thina thalassēs.
sentences.l:
So having spoken he chose out twenty men, the best,
and they set out to go to the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and picked out the twenty best men, and they set out for the swift ship and the shore of the sea.
sentences.n: ἐκρίνατο is an aorist middle of κρίνω, 'chose out for himself'; ἐείκοσι is the epic form of εἴκοσι 'twenty', with a prothetic ε-; φῶτας is accusative plural of φώς 'man, hero'. βὰν δ’ ἰέναι, 'they went to go', pairs a finite unaugmented aorist with a complementary infinitive, an idiomatic Homeric way of saying simply 'they set out'; νῆα θοήν keeps the house-fixed 'swift ship'.

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν οὖν πάμπρωτον ἁλὸς βένθοσδε ἔρυσσαν,
ἐν δ’ ἱστόν τ’ ἐτίθεντο καὶ ἱστία νηὶ μελαίνῃ,
ἠρτύναντο δ’ ἐρετμὰ τροποῖς ἐν δερματίνοισιν,
πάντα κατὰ μοῖραν, ἀνά θ’ ἱστία λευκὰ πέτασσαν·
sentences.tr:
nēa men oun pamprōton halos benthosde eryssan,
en d’ histon t’ etithento kai histia nēi melainēi,
ērtynanto d’ eretma tropois en dermatinoisin,
panta kata moiran, ana th’ histia leuka petassan·
sentences.l:
The ship, then, first of all, into the depths of the sea they drew,
and in it they set the mast and the sails, in the black ship,
and they fitted the oars into the leathern thongs,
all according to what is fitting, and they spread the white sails;
sentences.i: First of all they drew the ship down into the depths of the sea, set the mast and sails in the black ship, fitted the oars into their leather thongs, everything as was fitting, and spread the white sails;
sentences.n: βένθοσδε, 'to the deep', carries the directional suffix -δε; ἐρύω 'drag, haul' describes launching a beached ship. τρόποι are leather loops or thongs on the gunwale that held the oars in place, a detail of Homeric ship-fitting technique. κατὰ μοῖραν, 'according to what is fitting', is the already house-fixed adverbial phrase for correct, orderly procedure. The whole passage is a type-scene of launching a ship, reused with small variations elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t: τεύχεα δέ σφ’ ἤνεικαν ὑπέρθυμοι θεράποντες.
sentences.tr: teuchea de sph’ ēneikan hyperthymoi therapontes.
sentences.l: And their gear the high-spirited attendants carried for them.
sentences.i: And their high-spirited attendants brought their gear aboard.
sentences.n: ἤνεικαν is an augmented aorist of φέρω, built on the epic alternative root ἐνεικ- (contrast the unaugmented ἔνεικα); σφ’ is the enclitic dative plural, 'for them'. ὑπέρθυμος 'high-spirited' is a general term of praise for retainers here, without special reference to mood; τεύχεα are the weapons and equipment needed for the coming ambush.

sentences.t: ὑψοῦ δ’ ἐν νοτίῳ τήν γ’ ὥρμισαν, ἐκ δ’ ἔβαν αὐτοί·
sentences.tr: hypsou d’ en notiōi tēn g’ hōrmisan, ek d’ eban autoi·
sentences.l: And high up, in the water, they moored it, and out stepped they themselves;
sentences.i: They moored it well out in the water, and themselves stepped ashore;
sentences.n: νότιος here is a technical term for the offshore anchorage in deep water, as against hauling a ship up onto the beach: ships kept ready for a quick departure were often moored this way. ὥρμισαν is aorist of ὁρμίζω 'moor, anchor'; ἔβαν is an augmented aorist of βαίνω (contrast the unaugmented βάν at 779).

sentences.t: ἔνθα δὲ δόρπον ἕλοντο, μένον δ’ ἐπὶ ἕσπερον ἐλθεῖν.
sentences.tr: entha de dorpon helonto, menon d’ epi hesperon elthein.
sentences.l: There they took their meal, and waited for evening to come.
sentences.i: There they took their evening meal, and waited for evening to come.
sentences.n: δόρπον is the main evening meal; ἕλοντο is an unaugmented aorist middle of αἱρέω, 'took for themselves'. μένον ... ἐλθεῖν, 'waited for (evening) to come', uses the infinitive to express what they are waiting for. The twenty men time their ambush for nightfall, so as not to be seen — a detail that matters as the plot unfolds.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ὑπερωίῳ αὖθι περίφρων Πηνελόπεια
κεῖτ’ ἄρ’ ἄσιτος, ἄπαστος ἐδητύος ἠδὲ ποτῆτος,
ὁρμαίνουσ’ ἤ οἱ θάνατον φύγοι υἱὸς ἀμύμων,
ἦ ὅ γ’ ὑπὸ μνηστῆρσιν ὑπερφιάλοισι δαμείη.
sentences.tr:
hē d’ hyperōiōi authi periphrōn Pēnelopeia
keit’ ar’ asitos, apastos edētyos ēde potētos,
hormainous’ ē hoi thanaton phygoi huios amymōn,
ē ho g’ hypo mnēstērsin hyperphialoisi dameiē.
sentences.l:
But she, meanwhile, in the upper chamber, circumspect Penelope,
lay there fasting, tasting neither food nor drink,
pondering whether her blameless son might escape death,
or whether he might be overcome by the overweening suitors.
sentences.i: Meanwhile circumspect Penelope lay there in her upper room, fasting and tasting neither food nor drink, wondering whether her blameless son would escape death or be overcome by the overweening suitors.
sentences.n: περίφρων Πηνελόπεια is the house-fixed epithet 'circumspect Penelope', used regardless of context. ἄσιτος and ἄπαστος are near-synonyms, 'without food' and 'tasting nothing', piled up for emphasis. ὁρμαίνω 'ponder, turn over in the mind' here introduces an indirect double question with ἤ ... ἦ, 'whether ... or'. ἀμύμων 'blameless' is a stock epithet of disputed origin, given here to Telemachus; δαμείη is an aorist passive optative of δάμνημι 'overpower'.

sentences.t:
ὅσσα δὲ μερμήριξε λέων ἀνδρῶν ἐν ὁμίλῳ
δείσας, ὁππότε μιν δόλιον περὶ κύκλον ἄγωσι,
τόσσα μιν ὁρμαίνουσαν ἐπήλυθε νήδυμος ὕπνος·
sentences.tr:
hossa de mermērixe leōn andrōn en homilōi
deisas, hoppote min dolion peri kyklon agōsi,
tossa min hormainousan epēlythe nēdymos hypnos·
sentences.i: And just as a lion, penned in a ring of men, grows afraid as they close a treacherous circle around him — with just such racing thoughts sweet sleep came upon her as she pondered;
sentences.n: This simile compares Penelope's whirling anxiety to the wariness of a cornered lion; ὅσσα ... τόσσα, 'as many things as ... so many', is the correlative frame of the comparison. δόλιον περί κύκλον ἄγωσι pictures hunters driving a ring of men or nets around a trapped lion. νήδυμος ὕπνος, 'sweet sleep', is a stock formula for sleep as a release from care; the adjective's own formation, often linked by folk-etymology to ἡδύς 'sweet', is itself disputed.

sentences.t: εὗδε δ’ ἀνακλινθεῖσα, λύθεν δέ οἱ ἅψεα πάντα.
sentences.tr: heude d’ anaklintheisa, lythen de hoi hapsea panta.
sentences.l: And she slept, having leaned back, and all her limbs were loosened.
sentences.i: She slept, leaning back, and all her limbs relaxed.
sentences.n: ἀνακλινθεῖσα is an aorist passive participle of ἀνακλίνω, 'lean back'; λύθεν is an unaugmented aorist passive of λύω (Attic ἐλύθησαν). ἅψεα, 'limbs, joints', is a plural noun regularly paired with λύω to describe both sleep and death overtaking the body, a formula elsewhere applied to fallen warriors.

sentences.t: ἔνθ’ αὖτ’ ἄλλ’ ἐνόησε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr: enth’ aut’ all’ enoēse thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l: Then again another thing devised the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: Then, in her turn, the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, thought of something else.
sentences.n: This whole line already stood in an earlier part, introducing one of Athena's interventions; ἄλλο, 'another thing', is deliberately vague and kept as 'another thing' rather than sharpened to 'plan'. Here it introduces the sending of the dream-phantom that follows.

sentences.t:
εἴδωλον ποίησε, δέμας δ’ ἤικτο γυναικί,
Ἰφθίμῃ, κούρῃ μεγαλήτορος Ἰκαρίοιο,
τὴν Εὔμηλος ὄπυιε Φερῇς ἔνι οἰκία ναίων.
sentences.tr:
eidōlon poiēse, demas d’ ēikto gynaiki,
Iphthimēi, kourēi megalētoros Ikarioio,
tēn Eumēlos opuie Pherēis eni oikia naiōn.
sentences.l:
A phantom she made, and in body it was like a woman,
Iphthime, daughter of great-hearted Icarius,
whom Eumelus married, dwelling in a house in Pherae.
sentences.i: She made a phantom, shaped in body like a woman — Iphthime, daughter of great-hearted Icarius, whom Eumelus had married, living in his house in Pherae.
sentences.n: εἴδωλον, 'phantom, image, likeness', is new to this part and will recur through the scene; it is kept as 'phantom' every time. ἤικτο is a pluperfect-with-imperfect-sense of ἔοικα, 'was like, resembled', governing the dative γυναικί. Ἰφθίμη is Penelope's sister, otherwise unmentioned in the poem; Ἰκάριος is their father, brother of Tyndareus; Εὔμηλος and Φεραί (a town in Thessaly) are likewise new, given their ordinary English forms. ὄπυιε is imperfect of ὀπυίω 'have as a wife, be married to'.

sentences.t:
πέμπε δέ μιν πρὸς δώματ’ Ὀδυσσῆος θείοιο,
ἧος Πηνελόπειαν ὀδυρομένην γοόωσαν
παύσειε κλαυθμοῖο γόοιό τε δακρυόεντος.
sentences.tr:
pempe de min pros dōmat’ Odyssēos theioio,
hēos Pēnelopeian odyromenēn gooōsan
pauseie klauthmoio gooio te dakryoentos.
sentences.l:
And she sent it to the house of divine Odysseus,
so that it might stop Penelope, lamenting and wailing,
from weeping and tearful lament.
sentences.i: and sent it to the house of divine Odysseus, to stop Penelope's lamenting and wailing, her weeping and tearful grief.
sentences.n: θεῖος 'divine', applied here to Odysseus, is a distinct epithet-family from δῖος 'heavenly' (already reserved for him elsewhere) and θεοειδής 'godlike in form'; each is kept separate. ἧος is 'so that, until' (Attic ἕως); παύσειε is an aorist optative of παύω expressing purpose after a past main verb. The pile of near-synonyms for grief — ὀδυρομένην, γοόωσαν, κλαυθμοῖο, γόοιο, δακρυόεντος — is typical of this scene's emotional register.

sentences.t:
ἐς θάλαμον δ’ εἰσῆλθε παρὰ κληῖδος ἱμάντα,
στῆ δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.tr:
es thalamon d’ eisēlthe para klēidos himanta,
stē d’ ar’ hyper kephalēs, kai min pros mython eeipen·
sentences.l:
And into the chamber it entered by the thong of the bolt,
and it stood then above her head, and to her spoke a word:
sentences.i: It came into the bedchamber past the strap of the door-bolt, stood over her head, and spoke to her:
sentences.n: κληῖδος ἱμάντα, 'the thong of the bolt', is the leather strap used to work a door-latch from outside; the phantom slips through this narrow gap rather than opening the door, a detail confirmed again at 838 when it leaves the same way. ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς στῆναι, 'to stand over the head', is the regular Homeric posture of a dream-figure appearing to a sleeper; ἔειπεν is an augmented aorist built on the same stem as εἶπον, with the augment left visible before the (already contracted) stem, unlike the shorter, unaugmented εἶπε(ν).

sentences.t: εὕδεις, Πηνελόπεια, φίλον τετιημένη ἦτορ;
sentences.tr: heudeis, Pēnelopeia, philon tetiēmenē ētor;
sentences.l: “Do you sleep, Penelope, your dear heart grieving?
sentences.i: “Are you asleep, Penelope, and grieving in your heart?
sentences.n: τετιημένη is a perfect passive participle, 'worn down, distressed', with φίλον ἦτορ as an accusative of respect, 'as to your dear heart' — φίλος here functions almost as 'your own', as regularly with parts of the body. The line opens the phantom's speech as a gentle, almost teasing question, since of course Penelope is asleep and dreaming even as she is addressed.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν σ’ οὐδὲ ἐῶσι θεοὶ ῥεῖα ζώοντες
κλαίειν οὐδ’ ἀκάχησθαι, ἐπεί ῥ’ ἔτι νόστιμός ἐστι
σὸς παῖς·
sentences.tr:
ou men s’ oude eōsi theoi rheia zōontes
klaiein oud’ akachēsthai, epei rh’ eti nostimos esti
sos pais·
sentences.i: The gods who live at ease do not want you to weep or grieve, since your son is still to come safely home;
sentences.n: Ῥεῖα ζώοντες, 'living at ease', is the standing formula for the gods' untroubled existence, set against mortal suffering. ἐῶσι is present indicative of ἐάω 'allow, let'. νόστιμός ἐστι, literally 'is of a homecoming, is due to return', echoes the already-fixed formula νόστιμον ἦμαρ 'the homecoming day', built here on the related adjective.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γάρ τι θεοῖς ἀλιτήμενός ἐστι.
sentences.tr: ou men gar ti theois alitēmenos esti.
sentences.l: for he is not at all one who has sinned against the gods.”
sentences.i: for he has done the gods no wrong.”
sentences.n: ἀλιτήμενος is a perfect middle/passive participle of ἀλιταίνω, 'sin against, offend', with the dative θεοῖς. The phantom's assurance rests on the standard Homeric logic that a man's fortune reflects his standing with the gods — the same reasoning Eurycleia used earlier in this part.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα περίφρων Πηνελόπεια,
ἡδὺ μάλα κνώσσουσ’ ἐν ὀνειρείῃσι πύλῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
tēn d’ ēmeibet’ epeita periphrōn Pēnelopeia,
hēdy mala knōssous’ en oneireiēisi pylēisin·
sentences.l:
Her then answered circumspect Penelope,
slumbering very sweetly at the gates of dreams;
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope answered her, slumbering sweetly there at the gates of dreams;
sentences.n: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα and περίφρων Πηνελόπεια both keep their house-fixed wording; τήν here refers back to the phantom, imagined and addressed as a woman despite the grammatically neuter εἴδωλον. ὀνειρείῃσι πύλῃσιν, 'at the gates of dreams', is the same image Homer later elaborates, in Book 19, into twin gates of horn and of ivory for true and false dreams; here it appears in its simpler, unelaborated form. κνώσσω is 'slumber, sleep deeply'.

sentences.t: τίπτε, κασιγνήτη, δεῦρ’ ἤλυθες;
sentences.tr: tipte, kasignētē, deur’ ēlythes;
sentences.l: “Why, sister, have you come here?
sentences.i: “Why have you come here, sister?
sentences.n: τίπτε contracts τί ποτε, 'why ever, why then'; κασιγνήτη, 'sister', addresses the phantom as Iphthime, whom Penelope in her dream takes to be her real sister. ἤλυθες is an augmented aorist of ἔρχομαι, built on the epic root ἐλυθ- (Attic ἦλθες is the corresponding augmented form on the root ἐλθ-).

sentences.t:
οὔ τι πάρος γε
πωλέ’, ἐπεὶ μάλα πολλὸν ἀπόπροθι δώματα ναίεις·
sentences.tr:
ou ti paros ge
pōle’, epei mala pollon apoprothi dōmata naieis·
sentences.l:
not at all before now
have you come, since very far off you dwell in your house;
sentences.i: You have never come before, since you live so very far away;
sentences.n: πωλέ(ο) is imperfect of πωλέομαι, 'come habitually, frequent', with πάρος γε, 'before now', stressing that the visit is unprecedented. ἀπόπροθι, 'far off', is reinforced by μάλα πολλόν, 'very much so' — in her dream-logic Penelope registers the oddity of the visit before turning to her own grief.

sentences.t:
καί με κέλεαι παύσασθαι ὀιζύος ἠδ’ ὀδυνάων
πολλέων, αἵ μ’ ἐρέθουσι κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
sentences.tr:
kai me keleai pausasthai oizyos ēd’ odynaōn
polleōn, hai m’ erethousi kata phrena kai kata thymon,
sentences.l:
and you bid me cease from misery and from pains,
many, which stir me up in mind and in heart,
sentences.i: and you tell me to leave off the misery and the many pains that torment my mind and my heart —
sentences.n: κέλεαι is present middle of κέλομαι 'bid, urge'; ἐρέθουσι 'stir up, provoke' describes the pains as actively goading her. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν, 'in mind and in heart', is the house-fixed formula for inward feeling. The sentence is cut here at a comma, since carried through to its natural stop it would run past four lines; it continues directly into the relative clause about her lost husband.

sentences.t:
ἣ πρὶν μὲν πόσιν ἐσθλὸν ἀπώλεσα θυμολέοντα,
παντοίῃς ἀρετῇσι κεκασμένον ἐν Δαναοῖσιν,
ἐσθλόν, τοῦ κλέος εὐρὺ καθ’ Ἑλλάδα καὶ μέσον Ἄργος·
sentences.tr:
hē prin men posin esthlon apōlesa thymoleonta,
pantoiēis aretēisi kekasmenon en Danaoisin,
esthlon, tou kleos eury kath’ Hellada kai meson Argos·
sentences.i: I, who first lost a noble, lion-hearted husband, a man distinguished among the Greeks by virtues of every kind, noble, whose fame spread wide through Hellas and the middle of Argos;
sentences.n: These three lines already stood entire, word for word, in an earlier part, where Penelope used them of Odysseus before the suitors; the same English is kept here, in her second telling of the same grief to the figure she takes for her sister. θυμολέων, 'lion-hearted', joins θυμός to λέων; κεκασμένον is a perfect participle of καίνυμαι, 'excel, be distinguished'.

sentences.t:
νῦν αὖ παῖς ἀγαπητὸς ἔβη κοίλης ἐπὶ νηός,
νήπιος, οὔτε πόνων ἐὺ εἰδὼς οὔτ’ ἀγοράων.
sentences.tr:
nyn au pais agapētos ebē koilēs epi nēos,
nēpios, oute ponōn ey eidōs out’ agoraōn.
sentences.l:
and now again my beloved son has gone upon a hollow ship,
foolish, knowing well neither hardships nor assemblies.
sentences.i: and now my beloved son has gone off in a hollow ship, foolish as he is, with no experience yet of hardship or of public assembly.
sentences.n: ἀγαπητός, 'beloved', often marks an only or especially cherished child, as Telemachus is. νήπιος, 'foolish, without understanding' (literally 'not [yet] speaking'), is a recurring judgment on Telemachus's inexperience in the poem's early books. κοίλης ... νηός keeps the house-fixed 'hollow ship'; ἐὺ εἰδώς, 'knowing well', is negated across two genitives, πόνων and ἀγοράων.

sentences.t: τοῦ δὴ ἐγὼ καὶ μᾶλλον ὀδύρομαι ἤ περ ἐκείνου·
sentences.tr: tou dē egō kai mallon odyromai ē per ekeinou·
sentences.l: For him indeed I lament even more than for that one;
sentences.i: For him I grieve even more than for my husband;
sentences.n: τοῦ and ἐκείνου are both genitives governed by ὀδύρομαι, 'grieve for'; ἐκείνου, 'that one', points back to her dead husband just described, while τοῦ, resuming παῖς, is her son. ἤ περ intensifies the comparison, 'even more than'.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ἀμφιτρομέω καὶ δείδια, μή τι πάθῃσιν,
ἢ ὅ γε τῶν ἐνὶ δήμῳ, ἵν’ οἴχεται, ἢ ἐνὶ πόντῳ·
sentences.tr:
tou d’ amphitromeō kai deidia, mē ti pathēisin,
ē ho ge tōn eni dēmōi, hin’ oichetai, ē eni pontōi·
sentences.l:
and for him I tremble all about and I fear, lest he suffer something,
whether he, among those in the land where he has gone, or on the sea;
sentences.i: I tremble for him and am afraid that he may come to harm, whether among the people of the land he has gone to, or out on the sea;
sentences.n: ἀμφιτρομέω, 'tremble all around, tremble on his account', is a rare compound built on τρέμω. πάθῃσιν is a subjunctive in -ησι after the fear-clause μή. δῆμος here means the local population or country of wherever Telemachus is visiting, set against the open sea.

sentences.t:
δυσμενέες γὰρ πολλοὶ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ μηχανόωνται,
ἱέμενοι κτεῖναι πρὶν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
dysmenees gar polloi ep’ autōi mēchanoōntai,
hiemenoi kteinai prin patrida gaian hikesthai.
sentences.l:
for many enemies against him are contriving,
eager to kill him before he reaches his fatherland.”
sentences.i: for many enemies are plotting against him, eager to kill him before he reaches his native land.”
sentences.n: δυσμενέες, 'ill-disposed', is used substantivally for 'enemies'; μηχανόωνται is an uncontracted (diectasis) form of μηχανῶνται, 'contrive, devise'. ἱέμενοι, present participle of ἵημι, means 'eager, intent'. This closes Penelope's speech, and by dramatic irony names exactly the plot Antinous's men are now carrying out — information the waking Penelope cannot actually have.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενον προσέφη εἴδωλον ἀμαυρόν·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenon prosephē eidōlon amauron·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed the dim phantom:
sentences.i: In answer the dim phantom said to her:
sentences.n: The reply-formula τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη is already house-fixed; here the participle stands in its neuter form ἀπαμειβόμενον, agreeing grammatically with the neuter εἴδωλον rather than with τήν, though the same English rendering is kept. ἀμαυρόν, 'dim, faint, indistinct', is an ordinary word here, describing the phantom's shadowy insubstantiality. This exact line recurs unchanged at 835.

sentences.t: θάρσει, μηδέ τι πάγχυ μετὰ φρεσὶ δείδιθι λίην·
sentences.tr: tharsei, mēde ti panchy meta phresi deidithi liēn·
sentences.l: “Take heart, and do not at all in your mind be too greatly afraid;
sentences.i: “Take heart, and do not be too afraid in your mind;
sentences.n: θάρσει is a present imperative of θαρσέω, 'be of good courage'; δείδιθι is a rare perfect imperative of δείδω 'fear', with πάγχυ ... λίην piling up two intensifiers, 'altogether ... too much'. μετὰ φρεσί, 'among your wits, in your mind', is a variant of the more usual κατὰ φρένα.

sentences.t:
τοίη γάρ οἱ πομπὸς ἅμ’ ἔρχεται, ἥν τε καὶ ἄλλοι
ἀνέρες ἠρήσαντο παρεστάμεναι, δύναται γάρ,
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη·
sentences.tr:
toiē gar hoi pompos ham’ erchetai, hēn te kai alloi
aneres ērēsanto parestamenai, dynatai gar,
Pallas Athēnaiē·
sentences.i: for such a guide travels with him as other men too have prayed to have stand at their side, since she has the power to do it — Pallas Athena;
sentences.n: τοίη ... ἥν, 'such a one ... whom', is a correlative construction. πομπός, 'escort, guide', is a technical term for divine guidance on a journey; ἠρήσαντο is aorist middle of ἀράομαι 'prayed'; παρεστάμεναι is a perfect infinitive of παρίστημι used with present force, 'to stand beside'. δύναται γάρ, 'for she is able', delays the name itself for one more clause — a favorite Homeric device of suspended identification.

sentences.t: σὲ δ’ ὀδυρομένην ἐλεαίρει·
sentences.tr: se d’ odyromenēn eleairei·
sentences.l: and you, lamenting, she pities;
sentences.i: and she pities you in your grief;
sentences.n: ἐλεαίρω 'pity, feel compassion for' (an epic by-form of ἐλεέω) takes its object directly in the accusative; ὀδυρομένην, a present participle, 'as you lament', agrees with σέ.

sentences.t: ἣ νῦν με προέηκε τεῒν τάδε μυθήσασθαι.
sentences.tr: hē nyn me proeēke teïn tade mythēsasthai.
sentences.l: she it is who now sent me forth to tell you these things.”
sentences.i: and it was she who sent me now to tell you this.”
sentences.n: προέηκε is an unaugmented aorist of προΐημι, 'send forth'; τεῒν is an old dative form of σύ, 'to you' (Attic σοί), found chiefly in prayer- and speech-formulas. μυθήσασθαι is an aorist infinitive of μυθέομαι, 'tell, relate', closing the phantom's first speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ aute proseeipe periphrōn Pēnelopeia·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: The reply-formula τὸν/τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε is already house-fixed for masculine referents; here, exactly as at 742, it is applied with the feminine pronoun, referring back to the phantom, and περίφρων Πηνελόπεια again keeps its fixed wording.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ θεός ἐσσι θεοῖό τε ἔκλυες αὐδῆς,
εἰ δ’ ἄγε μοι καὶ κεῖνον ὀιζυρὸν κατάλεξον,
ἤ που ἔτι ζώει καὶ ὁρᾷ φάος ἠελίοιο,
ἦ ἤδη τέθνηκε καὶ εἰν Ἀίδαο δόμοισι.
sentences.tr:
ei men dē theos essi theoio te eklyes audēs,
ei d’ age moi kai keinon oizyron katalexon,
ē pou eti zōei kai horāi phaos ēelioio,
ē ēdē tethnēke kai ein Aidao domoisi.
sentences.l:
“If indeed you are a god, and have heard a god's voice,
come then, tell me also of that wretched man,
whether he still lives somewhere and sees the light of the sun,
or whether he is already dead and in the house of Hades.”
sentences.i: “If you are indeed a goddess, and have heard the voice of a god, come, tell me also of that unhappy man — whether he is still alive somewhere and sees the light of the sun, or whether he is already dead and in the house of Hades.”
sentences.n: ἐσσι is the epic 2nd singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ); εἰ δ’ ἄγε, 'come now', is a fixed formula of urging, already fixed elsewhere as part of a longer line. κατάλεξον is an aorist imperative of καταλέγω, 'recount, tell in order'. The double indirect question ἤ ... ἦ, 'whether ... or', mirrors the same construction Penelope used of Telemachus at 789–790; Ἀίδαο δόμοισι, 'in the house of Hades', is a standard periphrasis for death.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενον προσέφη εἴδωλον ἀμαυρόν·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ apameibomenon prosephē eidōlon amauron·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed the dim phantom:
sentences.i: In answer the dim phantom said to her:
sentences.n: This line repeats 824 verbatim, and the English is kept identical both times, as the house style requires for a repeated line.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν τοι κεῖνόν γε διηνεκέως ἀγορεύσω,
ζώει ὅ γ’ ἦ τέθνηκε·
sentences.tr:
ou men toi keinon ge diēnekeōs agoreusō,
zōei ho g’ ē tethnēke·
sentences.l:
“I will not tell you of that man continuously, straight through,
whether he lives or he is dead;
sentences.i: “I will not tell you the whole plain truth about him, whether he is alive or dead;
sentences.n: διηνεκέως, 'continuously, from end to end', qualifies ἀγορεύσω, 'I will not tell of him at full length'. The phantom pointedly refuses the very question just asked: οὐ ... ἀγορεύσω governs the indirect question ζώει ... ἦ τέθνηκε with no subordinating conjunction, a vivid direct-question form kept inside indirect speech, typical of Homeric style.

sentences.t: κακὸν δ’ ἀνεμώλια βάζειν.
sentences.tr: kakon d’ anemōlia bazein.
sentences.l: and it is a bad thing to babble idle words.”
sentences.i: for it is no good thing to talk idly.”
sentences.n: ἀνεμώλια, literally 'windy things' (from ἄνεμος 'wind'), means 'idle, empty words'; βάζω is 'chatter, babble'. The phantom's evasive proverb ends its second speech, refusing outright to say whether Odysseus lives — a calculated divine reticence.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὸν σταθμοῖο παρὰ κληῖδα λιάσθη
ἐς πνοιὰς ἀνέμων.
sentences.tr:
hōs eipon stathmoio para klēida liasthē
es pnoias anemōn.
sentences.l:
So having spoken, from the door-post, by the bolt, it slipped away,
into the blowing of the winds.
sentences.i: So it spoke, and slipped away by the door-bolt into the blowing of the winds.
sentences.n: εἰπόν is the neuter nominative aorist participle 'having spoken', agreeing grammatically with the neuter εἴδωλον (where a personal subject would take the masculine εἰπών) — a small but telling detail: Homer's grammar keeps calling the dream-figure 'it' even while it acts and speaks as 'she', just as with ἀπαμειβόμενον at 824 and 835. λιάσθη is an aorist passive of λιάζομαι, 'slip away, glide off'; the phantom leaves by the very door-fastening through which it entered at 802.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἐξ ὕπνου ἀνόρουσε
κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ex hypnou anorouse
kourē Ikarioio·
sentences.l:
And she started up out of sleep,
the daughter of Icarius;
sentences.i: And Icarius's daughter started up out of her sleep;
sentences.n: ἀνόρουσε is aorist of ἀνορούω, 'spring up, start up'. κούρη Ἰκαρίοιο, 'the daughter of Icarius', here designates Penelope herself, not, as at 797, her sister Iphthime — an ambiguity the shared patronymic allows, since Icarius is father to both women.

sentences.t:
φίλον δέ οἱ ἦτορ ἰάνθη,
ὥς οἱ ἐναργὲς ὄνειρον ἐπέσσυτο νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ.
sentences.tr:
philon de hoi ētor ianthē,
hōs hoi enarges oneiron epessyto nyktos amolgōi.
sentences.l:
and her dear heart was warmed,
since a clear dream had come upon her in the dead of night.
sentences.i: and her heart was warmed, because a vivid dream had come to her in the depths of the night.
sentences.n: ἰάνθη is an aorist passive of ἰαίνω, 'warm, cheer, gladden'. ἐναργές, 'clear, vivid', describes a dream felt as truly present rather than a vague fancy. νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ, literally 'in the milking-time of night', is an old poetic phrase for deep night; ἀμολγός is barely attested outside this phrase, and its original sense is disputed.

sentences.t:
μνηστῆρες δ’ ἀναβάντες ἐπέπλεον ὑγρὰ κέλευθα
Τηλεμάχῳ φόνον αἰπὺν ἐνὶ φρεσὶν ὁρμαίνοντες.
sentences.tr:
mnēstēres d’ anabantes epepleon hygra keleutha
Tēlemachōi phonon aipyn eni phresin hormainontes.
sentences.l:
And the suitors, having embarked, were sailing over the watery ways,
for Telemachus contriving steep murder in their minds.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the suitors had embarked and were sailing over the watery ways, plotting steep death for Telemachus in their hearts.
sentences.n: ὑγρὰ κέλευθα, 'the watery ways', is the already house-fixed phrase for the open sea. φόνον αἰπύν, 'steep murder', adapts the fixed formula αἰπὺς ὄλεθρος 'steep destruction' to the near-synonym φόνος. ὁρμαίνοντες again picks up the verb of anxious pondering already used of Penelope (789, 793), tying the suitors' scheming directly to her fears for her son.

sentences.t:
ἔστι δέ τις νῆσος μέσσῃ ἁλὶ πετρήεσσα,
μεσσηγὺς Ἰθάκης τε Σάμοιό τε παιπαλοέσσης,
Ἀστερίς, οὐ μεγάλη·
sentences.tr:
esti de tis nēsos messēi hali petrēessa,
messēgys Ithakēs te Samoio te paipaloessēs,
Asteris, ou megalē·
sentences.i: There is a rocky island out in the middle of the strait, between Ithaca and rugged Same, called Asteris, not a large one;
sentences.n: μέσσῃ ἁλί, 'in the middle of the sea', situates the island in the strait. Σάμος here is the island later called Same, near Ithaca and quite distinct from the Aegean Samos, and takes its already fixed familiar form 'Same'; παιπαλόεσσα 'rugged' is a standing epithet of rough terrain. Ἀστερίς, 'Asteris', is new to this part; it is usually identified with the small islet now called Daskalio, in the channel between Ithaca and Cephallenia.

sentences.t:
λιμένες δ’ ἔνι ναύλοχοι αὐτῇ
ἀμφίδυμοι·
sentences.tr:
limenes d’ eni naulochoi autēi
amphidymoi·
sentences.l:
and harbours, fit for ships, are on it,
two-fold;
sentences.i: and it has two harbours where ships can lie,
sentences.n: ναύλοχος, 'ship-sheltering, fit to anchor ships in', is a transparent compound of ναῦς and the root of λόχος. ἀμφίδυμοι, 'double, with an entrance on each side', describes a harbour open at both ends — a natural point for an ambush, since a ship lying there could watch both approaches to Ithaca.

sentences.t: τῇ τόν γε μένον λοχόωντες Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.tr: tēi ton ge menon lochoōntes Achaioi.
sentences.l: there for him the Achaeans, lying in wait, waited.
sentences.i: there the Achaeans lay in wait for him, watching.
sentences.n: λοχόωντες, a present participle of λοχάω 'lie in ambush' (built on λόχος 'ambush, band lying in wait', the same root just used in ναύλοχος), makes explicit the purpose already implied by the double harbour. τῇ, 'there', points back to Asteris; the part ends with the suitors poised in ambush, a deliberately suspended note before the story returns to Telemachus.
